note: ten episode briefs; facts from NASA Space Place pages; quotes are the pages' words (segments joined by ' … '), revised after the first fact-gate review (2026-11-03), which found four quotes not on their pages

exchanges.q: Why is the sky blue, Ravi?
exchanges.a: Air scatters blue light more than reds and yellows, so blue reaches us from every direction.
At sunset the light crosses much more air. Even more of the blue is scattered away, and the reds and yellows come straight through.

f1.claim: Air molecules scatter blue light in all directions, more than other colours, so the sky looks blue.

source.title: NASA Space Place: Why is the sky blue?
source.quote: Blue light is scattered in all directions by the tiny molecules of air in Earth's atmosphere. Blue is scattered more than other colors because it travels as shorter, smaller waves.

f2.claim: At sunset light passes through more air; more blue is scattered, leaving reds and yellows.

source.title: NASA Space Place: Why is the sky blue?
source.quote: As the Sun gets lower in the sky, its light is passing through more of the atmosphere to reach you. … Even more of the blue light is scattered, allowing the reds and yellows to pass straight through to your eyes.

titles: Why is the sky blue?
Why are sunsets orange when the sky is blue?
packaging.by: series brief (written by Claude, checked by title.set)

episodes.title: Does the Moon really change shape?

exchanges.q: Why does the Moon change shape?
exchanges.a: It doesn't. The Moon only reflects sunlight, and we see more or less of its lit side as it goes around us.

exchanges.q: How long until it looks the same again?
exchanges.a: About twenty-nine and a half days from one new moon to the next.

f1.claim: The Moon's shape does not change; it makes no light, and our view of its sunlit part changes as it goes around Earth.

source.title: NASA Space Place: Moon phases
source.quote: The shape of the Moon isn’t changing throughout the month. … The Moon does not produce its own light. … What you may have heard referred to as “moonlight” is actually just sunlight reflecting off of the Moon’s surface. … On Earth, our view of the illuminated part of the Moon changes each night, depending on where the Moon is in its orbit, or path, around Earth.

f2.claim: From one new moon to the next takes about 29.5 days.

source.title: NASA Space Place: Moon phases
source.quote: it takes about 29.5 days to go from one new moon to the next new moon.

titles: Does the Moon really change shape?
Why does the Moon look different each night?
packaging.by: series brief (written by Claude, checked by title.set)

exchanges.q: What's a light-year? Is it a long time?
exchanges.a: It's a distance: how far light travels in one year. About nine trillion kilometres!
Seen as they were long ago. Light from some stars left them thousands of years ago. Looking far is looking back in time.

f1.claim: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year, about 9 trillion km.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is a light-year?
source.quote: about 6 trillion miles (9 trillion km)

f2.claim: Distant objects are seen as they were in the past; some stars we see are thousands of light-years away.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is a light-year?
source.quote: When we use powerful telescopes to look at distant objects in space, we are actually looking back in time. … The farther an object is, the farther in the past we see it. … All of the other stars we can see with our eyes are farther, some even thousands of light-years away.

titles: What is a light-year?
Is a light-year a time or a distance?
packaging.by: series brief (written by Claude, checked by title.set)

exchanges.q: How hot is the Sun inside?
exchanges.a: Its core gets as hot as twenty-seven million degrees Fahrenheit.
It's so big that its gravity squeezes the hydrogen inside really hard. The hydrogen smashes together and turns into helium, and that gives off energy.

f1.claim: The Sun's core gets as hot as 27 million degrees Fahrenheit.

source.title: NASA Space Place: Where Does the Sun's Energy Come From?
source.quote: as hot as 27 million degrees Fahrenheit

f2.claim: The Sun is so big that its gravity and pressure make hydrogen atoms collide and fuse into helium, releasing energy.

source.title: NASA Space Place: Where Does the Sun's Energy Come From?
source.quote: The short answer is that it is big. … the hydrogen atoms collide with enough force that they literally meld into a new element—helium. This process—called nuclear fusion—releases energy

titles: How hot is the Sun inside?
Why is the Sun so hot?
packaging.by: series brief (written by Claude, checked by title.set)

exchanges.q: Is a shooting star a falling star?
exchanges.a: No. It's a space rock rushing into our air. The bright streak is the glowing hot air as the rock zips through.
That's when Earth meets lots of those rocks at once.

f1.claim: A shooting star is a space rock entering the atmosphere; the bright streak is the glowing hot air around it.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is a meteor shower?
source.quote: A meteor is a space rock—or meteoroid—that enters Earth's atmosphere. … That bright streak is not actually the rock, but rather the glowing hot air as the hot rock zips through the atmosphere.

f2.claim: When Earth meets many meteoroids at once, it is a meteor shower.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is a meteor shower?
source.quote: When Earth encounters many meteoroids at once, we call it a meteor shower.

titles: What is a shooting star?
Is a shooting star really a star?
packaging.by: series brief (written by Claude, checked by title.set)

exchanges.a: A regular, repeating path one thing takes around another in space.

exchanges.q: Why doesn't the Space Station fall?
exchanges.a: It is always falling! But it moves sideways so fast that it keeps missing Earth. It goes round in about ninety minutes.

f1.claim: An orbit is a regular, repeating path one object in space takes around another.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is an orbit?
source.quote: a regular, repeating path that one object in space takes around another one

f2.claim: A satellite is always falling toward the planet but moves sideways fast enough to miss; the ISS circles Earth in about 90 minutes.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is an orbit?
source.quote: When these forces are balanced, the object is always falling toward the planet, but because it's moving sideways fast enough, it never hits the planet. … The International Space Station is in low Earth orbit, or LEO. … One complete orbit in LEO takes about 90 minutes.

titles: Why don't satellites fall down?
Why doesn't the Space Station fall?
packaging.by: series brief (written by Claude, checked by title.set)

exchanges.q: Is it summer when we're close to the Sun?
exchanges.a: No. Earth's tilt makes the seasons. When our half leans towards the Sun, it's summer.
In January! That's winter in the north.

f1.claim: Earth's tilted axis causes the seasons, not its distance from the Sun.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What causes the seasons?
source.quote: Earth's tilted axis causes the seasons

f2.claim: Earth is closest to the Sun in January, winter in the Northern Hemisphere.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What causes the seasons?
source.quote: perihelion (when we are closest) occurs in January

titles: What causes the seasons?
Is summer when Earth is closest to the Sun?

exchanges.a: A huge collection of gas, dust and billions of stars, held together by gravity.
Yes, the Milky Way. And there are so many galaxies, nobody can count them all yet!

f1.claim: A galaxy is a huge collection of gas, dust and billions of stars held together by gravity.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is a galaxy?
source.quote: A galaxy is a huge collection of gas, dust, and billions of stars and their solar systems, all held together by gravity.

f2.claim: We live in the Milky Way galaxy; there are so many galaxies that they cannot all be counted yet.

source.title: NASA Space Place: What is a galaxy?
source.quote: It’s a small part of the Milky Way Galaxy. … There are so many, we can’t even count them all yet!

titles: What is a galaxy?
Is the Milky Way a galaxy?

exchanges.a: Something gets in the way of sunlight. In a solar eclipse, the Moon's shadow falls on Earth.
Earth gets in the way of the light reaching the Moon, so the Moon gets darker.

f1.claim: In a solar eclipse the Moon blocks the Sun's light and casts its shadow on Earth.

source.title: NASA Space Place: Lunar Eclipses and Solar Eclipses
source.quote: An eclipse happens when a planet or a moon gets in the way of the Sun’s light. … solar eclipse happens when the Moon gets in the way of the Sun’s light and casts its shadow on Earth.

f2.claim: In a lunar eclipse Earth blocks the sunlight reaching the Moon, and the Moon gets darker.

source.title: NASA Space Place: Lunar Eclipses and Solar Eclipses
source.quote: During a lunar eclipse, Earth gets in the way of the Sun’s light hitting the Moon. … In a lunar eclipse, the Moon gets darker.

titles: What is an eclipse?
What happens in a solar eclipse?

episodes.title: How long is a day on other planets?

exchanges.q: Is a day always twenty-four hours?
exchanges.a: Only on Earth! Mars takes twenty-five hours, and Jupiter spins round in just ten.
Venus! It takes five thousand eight hundred and thirty-two hours to spin round just once.

f1.claim: Earth spins in 24 hours, Mars in 25, Jupiter in 10.

source.title: NASA Space Place: How long is one day on other planets?
source.quote: Earth takes 24 hours to complete one spin, and Mars takes 25 hours. The gas giants rotate really fast. Jupiter takes just 10 hours to complete one rotation.

f2.claim: Venus takes 5,832 hours to spin round once, the longest of the planets in NASA's table.

source.title: NASA Space Place: How long is one day on other planets?
source.quote: On Mercury a day lasts 1,408 hours, and on Venus it lasts 5,832 hours.

titles: How long is a day on other planets?
Which planet spins the slowest?
